questions.statement: Choose the passive voice sentence.
questions.context: A report describes who repainted a classroom.

options.text: The classroom was repainted last week.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Was' plus the past participle forms the passive in the past simple.

options.text: The classroom has repainted last week.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Has repainted' is the present perfect active; the passive would need 'has been repainted'.

options.text: The classroom repainted last week.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Repainted' in the simple form is active, because a transitive verb without 'by' is read as active.

options.text: The classroom was repainting last week.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Was repainting' is passive only if followed by 'by'; a bare gerund here makes the sentence incomplete.

questions.explanation:
The passive is built with a form of be plus the past participle, and a by-phrase is optional when the agent is unimportant.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the passive sentence in the present simple.
questions.context: A news item reports an event without naming who was responsible.

options.text: The bridge is building in 1790.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is building' would need a by-phrase to be passive, and without one it is ungrammatical.

options.text: The bridge is built in 1790.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Is' plus the past participle 'built' forms the present simple passive, which fits a completed construction.

options.text: The bridge built in 1790.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Built' is the past simple active; the passive in the past would be 'was built'.

options.text: The bridge builds in 1790.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Builds' is the active form, which would identify a builder and imply someone constructs the bridge.

questions.explanation:
Note that the participle and the base form of a verb can look identical, so the auxiliary be is what identifies the passive.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly includes the agent in a passive construction.
questions.context: A museum caption names the artist, so the agent is known.

options.text: The mural was painted by a local artist from Cusco.
options.feedback: Wrong. The extra information about Cusco is irrelevant to the caption and makes the by-phrase wordy without adding accuracy.

options.text: The mural was painted by a local.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'A local' is too vague to identify the agent, and it loses the professional description.

options.text: The mural was painted by a local artist.
options.feedback: Correct. 'By' introduces the agent that performed the action, which is what this caption needs.

options.text: The mural was painted of a local artist.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'By' introduces an agent, not a location, so 'by of' and 'by a place' are both incorrect.

questions.explanation:
The by-phrase is used when the agent matters, and it is followed by a person or organisation performing the action.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the correct passive question.
questions.context: A student needs a passive question for a school report.

options.text: The project was finished on time?
options.feedback: Wrong. This is a statement, and it lacks the inversion that a yes/no question requires.

options.text: Is the project finished on time?
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is finished' would place the project in the present, which does not match the reference to the deadline already passed.

options.text: Did the project finish on time?
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Did finish' is the active form of the question and implies an agent completed the project.

options.text: Was the project finished on time?
options.feedback: Correct. A passive question is formed by inverting the auxiliary 'was' and keeping the past participle, which is what this sentence does.

questions.explanation:
Passive questions invert the auxiliary form of be, exactly as active questions invert do, does or did.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the passive sentence in the present perfect.
questions.context: A reporter writes about an event in the present perfect.

options.text: The results have been published this morning.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Have been' plus the past participle forms the present perfect passive.

options.text: The results was published this morning.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Was' is the past simple and does not agree with the plural subject 'results'.

options.text: The results have been publish this morning.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Have been publish' lacks the past participle after the auxiliary 'been'.

options.text: The results have published this morning.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Have published' is the present perfect active, which would require a subject that publishes.

questions.explanation:
The present perfect passive is have been plus participle, and the participle is what marks the passive.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the passive sentence in the present continuous.
questions.context: A sign announces an ongoing activity carried out by someone else.

options.text: The road is repairing at the moment.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is repairing' without a by-phrase is not a passive construction at all.

options.text: The road is being repaired at the moment.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Is being' plus the past participle is the present continuous passive, and 'road' is singular so 'is' is correct.

options.text: The road are being repaired at the moment.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Are' would require a plural subject, and the subject here is the singular noun 'road'.

options.text: The road is being repair at the moment.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is being repair' lacks the past participle after 'being'.

questions.explanation:
The present continuous passive is am, is or are plus being plus the past participle, with correct subject-verb agreement.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence in which the passive is genuinely more appropriate than the active.
questions.context: A style guide explains when the passive is preferred.

options.text: The results still analyse.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Analyse' is the active third person singular and presents the results as the analyser.

options.text: The results are still analysing.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Are analysing' without a by-phrase is not a passive, and it would also need an agent to be grammatical.

options.text: The results are still being analysed.
options.feedback: Correct. The action is in progress and the agent is unstated, so the present continuous passive is the natural form.

options.text: The results are still analysed.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Are analysed' is the simple present passive, which loses the sense of an action currently under way.

questions.explanation:
The passive is preferred when the action matters more than the agent, and the continuous passive additionally marks the action as ongoing.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which statement best explains the difference in information between the two sentences?
questions.context: An editor compares an active and a passive version of the same fact.

options.text: The passive version implies that the agent is unknown, whereas the active version implies the action was illegitimate.
options.feedback: Wrong. The passive carries no implication of illegitimacy; that judgement would come from the wording, not from the voice.

options.text: The active version is less informative because active sentences cannot include time expressions.
options.feedback: Wrong. Both forms can carry time expressions; that is not what distinguishes them.

options.text: Both sentences convey identical information, since the passive does not remove the agent.
options.feedback: Wrong. Passivising does remove or demote the agent, so the two sentences are not informationally identical.

options.text: The passive version foregrounds the action and leaves the agent unstated, while the active version identifies who performed it.
options.feedback: Correct. This describes the informational contrast accurately: passivising removes the agent from prominence.

questions.explanation:
Voice choice is a rhetorical decision, and describing it requires stating what changes in emphasis rather than asserting that the forms are identical.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the passive sentence in the past continuous.
questions.context: A process description covers a sequence of actions.

options.text: The letters were being signed while I was waiting.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Were being' plus the past participle is the past continuous passive, which matches the ongoing signing.

options.text: The letters are being signed while I was waiting.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Are being' is the present continuous passive and clashes with the past 'was waiting' in the main clause.

options.text: The letters were signed while I am waiting.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Were signed' would place the signing at a single past moment, and 'am waiting' does not match the past frame.

options.text: The letters were being sign while I was waiting.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Were being sign' lacks the past participle after 'being'.

questions.explanation:
Both clauses of a past continuous sentence need the past frame: the passive clause takes were being plus participle.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the passive sentence referring to the future.
questions.context: A summary describes a future event without naming who will act.

options.text: The new wing will be inaugurate in May.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will be inaugurate' lacks the past participle after 'be'.

options.text: The new wing will be inaugurated in May.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Will be' plus the past participle is the standard way to express a future passive without naming the agent.

options.text: The new wing are inaugurated in May.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Are' does not agree with the singular subject 'wing'.

options.text: The new wing will inaugurate in May.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Will inaugurate' is active and assigns the action to the wing, which cannot perform it.

questions.explanation:
Future passives rely on the modal will plus be plus the past participle, which is a very common structure in announcements.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the passive sentence in the past perfect continuous.
questions.context: A report describes an action continuing up to a past point.

options.text: The bridge had been repairing for a month before the rains began.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Had been repairing' would require a by-phrase to be passive, so it is not a passive form here.

options.text: The bridge had been under repair for a month before the rains begin.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'The rains begin' is present simple and does not match the past time frame.

options.text: The bridge had been under repair for a month before the rains began.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Had been' plus the participle phrase marks a passive process that was still continuing at that past point.

options.text: The bridge has been under repair for a month before the rains began.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Has been' is the present perfect, which cannot precede the past simple 'began'.

questions.explanation:
The past perfect continuous is formed with had been plus the participle or the prepositional phrase, as in 'under repair'.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the reason that best justifies using the passive in the sentence 'Mistakes were made.'
questions.context: A text asks why an action is done in the passive.

options.text: The passive is used when the subject of the active sentence is not a person.
options.feedback: Wrong. Passives regularly name people as agents, as in 'the poem was written by a student'.

options.text: The passive is used to make the sentence shorter by removing the participle.
options.feedback: Wrong. The passive is not chosen for length and does not remove the participle, which is essential to the form.

options.text: The passive is always required when the verb is a transitive one.
options.feedback: Wrong. Passive and active are both available for transitive verbs, so the transitivity of the verb is not a reason.

options.text: The agent is genuinely unknown or unimportant, so the sentence focuses on what happened rather than who did it.
options.feedback: Correct. This is the standard justification: the agent is unknown or not worth naming, so the focus stays on the event.

questions.explanation:
An explanation of voice choice should rest on emphasis and information, since the form itself has no other restriction.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the passive conditional sentence.
questions.context: An exam tests a passive conditional.

options.text: If the deadline were extended, the report could be finished.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Were extended' is the second conditional passive and 'could be finished' is the modal passive, so both clauses are grammatically passive.

options.text: If the deadline would be extended, the report could be finished.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Would be extended' in an if-clause is not the standard second conditional form.

options.text: If the deadline was extended, the report could finished.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Could finished' omits the auxiliary 'be' that the modal passive requires.

options.text: If the deadline were extend, the report could be finished.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Were extend' lacks the past participle after the auxiliary in the passive clause.

questions.explanation:
Conditionals can be passivised in both clauses, and the structure requires be plus participle in each passive element.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that correctly combines an active main clause with a passive subordinate clause.
questions.context: A report mixes active and passive to vary emphasis.

options.text: The council approved a plan that was draw up by two architects.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Was draw up' lacks the past participle after the auxiliary.

options.text: The council approved a plan that was drawn up by two architects.
options.feedback: Correct. The main clause is active and the relative clause is passive with 'was' plus the past participle, which is a standard combination.

options.text: The council approves a plan that was drawn up by two architects.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Approves' is present simple and conflicts with the past tense of the passive clause.

options.text: The council approved a plan that drew up by two architects.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'That drew up by' is not a passive clause and leaves the relative clause without a verb.

questions.explanation:
Mixing voices within one sentence is normal, and each clause must independently satisfy the requirements of its own voice.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the passive sentence with 'must' about the past.
questions.context: An exam tests a passive with a modal of deduction.

options.text: The letters must been stolen from the office.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Must been' omits the auxiliary 'have' that the perfect requires.

options.text: The letters must have stole from the office.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Must have stole' needs the past participle 'stolen' after the auxiliary 'have'.

options.text: The letters must have been stolen from the office.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Must have been' plus participle is a modal perfect passive expressing a deduction about a past event.

options.text: The letters must be stolen from the office last night.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Must be stolen' is a present deduction and cannot be combined with 'last night'.

questions.explanation:
Modal perfect passives are formed with modal plus have plus been plus the past participle, which encodes a deduction about the past.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence that is correct because the verb does not form a passive.
questions.context: A test checks knowledge of which verbs do not take the passive.

options.text: The news is spread quickly through the town.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is spread' attempts a passive from an intransitive verb and is not acceptable.

options.text: The news spreaded quickly through the town.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Spread' is already irregular or unchanged in this sense, so adding -ed is wrong.

options.text: The news was spread quickly through the town.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Was spread' treats the intransitive verb as if it were transitive and is not acceptable.

options.text: The news spread quickly through the town.
options.feedback: Correct. 'Spread' is an intransitive verb here and cannot take a passive, so the active form is the only option.

questions.explanation:
Verbs such as arrive, happen, occur, rise and fall have no passive form, and recognising them prevents a whole class of errors.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which statement is accurate about the sentence 'The window was broken'?
questions.context: A semantics exercise compares the agent in an active and a passive sentence.

options.text: The agent is unspecified, and context may or may not make it recoverable.
options.feedback: Correct. This correctly describes the ambiguity of an agentless passive, which is exactly why such sentences are avoided in precise writing.

options.text: The agent is revealed by the use of the past participle.
options.feedback: Wrong. The participle marks the passive, not the identity of the agent.

options.text: The agent cannot be a person under any circumstances.
options.feedback: Wrong. People are perfectly normal agents of breaking windows, so the restriction claimed here is false.

options.text: The agent is definitely the person reading the sentence.
options.feedback: Wrong. The reader supplies no agent, and the sentence works for a child, a pet or a storm.

questions.explanation:
An agentless passive leaves the doer genuinely unspecified, and that indeterminacy is a well-known property of the construction.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence in which every passive form is correct.
questions.context: An exam item tests a sequence of passives in different tenses.

options.text: The site is cleared, the fences were being repair, and the keys have been return.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is cleared' changes the time frame and 'being repair' and 'been return' both lack the participle.

options.text: The site was cleared, the fences were being repaired, and the keys have been returned.
options.feedback: Correct. All three clauses are correctly passivised: was cleared, were being repaired and have been returned.

options.text: The site had cleared, the fences were being repaired, and the keys have been returned.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Had cleared' is not a passive form, since the passive requires be plus the participle.

options.text: The site cleared, the fences were repaired, and the keys returned.
options.feedback: Wrong. Without an auxiliary, 'cleared', 'repaired' and 'returned' all read as active verbs.

questions.explanation:
A well-formed passive always depends on an auxiliary form of be plus a past participle, and that requirement holds in every tense.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence in which the auxiliary agrees correctly with the subject.
questions.context: A grammar task tests subject-verb agreement inside a passive clause.

options.text: The bags is packed and the tickets are print.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is' does not agree with 'bags' and 'are print' lacks the past participle.

options.text: The bags was packed and the tickets was printed.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Was' is singular and does not agree with the plural subject 'bags' in either clause.

options.text: The bags were packed and the tickets were printed.
options.feedback: Correct. Both subjects are plural, so each passive clause correctly takes 'were' plus the past participle.

options.text: The bags was packed and the tickets are printed.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Was packed' disagrees with 'bags' and the two clauses use inconsistent auxiliaries.

questions.explanation:
Passivising does not remove the obligation to make the auxiliary agree with the subject of each clause.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Choose the sentence in which the by-phrase changes the meaning rather than merely adding detail.
questions.context: An exam item tests the difference between two passive readings.

options.text: The song is written by a student from Lima.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Is written' describes a recurring present situation and changes the time frame.

options.text: The song was wrote by a student from Lima.
options.feedback: Wrong. 'Was wrote' lacks the past participle after the auxiliary.

options.text: The song was written by a piano.
options.feedback: Wrong. Naming a piano as the agent produces a comic or impossible reading, since an instrument cannot compose.

options.text: The song was written by a student from Lima.
options.feedback: Correct. Naming the writer as a person supports the reading that someone composed the song.

questions.explanation: Because the by-phrase names the agent, its choice determines whether the sentence is plausible, which is the point the item tests.
questions.subject: ingles
